utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. Please, Registry, call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: May we have for today the composition of the parties, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. Mark Harmon and Laurent Vuillemin for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is represented today by Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith, Tina Drolec, Alex Fielding, and Oonagh O'Connor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the absence of Judge Moloto, the Chamber will sit today 15 bis. And also, I would like to give to the parties some thoughts on to how should we proceed today. Yesterday, the issue of fresh evidence was raised by Mr. Lukic, and as I recall well, Mr. Lukic said that he would like to add some arguments to the case he presented. And, likewise, Mr. Harmon for the Prosecution said also that he would like to address the issue. So the Chamber has decided before they continue with the interrogation of the witness that was carried on yesterday by Mr. Harmon at the end of the session, the Chamber, I repeat, would like the parties to address the issue. I will recommend to the parties to be very concise, very precise, and also very brief so we could then have the arguments so the ruling of the Chamber could be done. Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we should be in private session for the arguments that we launched yesterday. I'm not sure, however, with regard to the nature of the documents that will be discussed, I believe that we should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Registrar, please let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honours, my arguments deal with Mr. Harmon's proposal with regard to XN 358. On this occasion, I would like to state that we as Mr. Perisic's Defence agree that Mladic's diaries is new information that reached the Prosecution after the end of the Prosecution case. If the Prosecution wishes to use Mladic's diaries, it has to file a request in keeping with the Prlic decision by the Appeals Chamber on the 26th of February, 2010, para 23. If the Prosecution can prove extraordinary circumstances in the interest of justice and the importance of such new documents, the Trial Chamber can then either agree to accept or refuse the use of such documents. In keeping with the same decision from the Prlic case, in each individual case, the Prosecution has to file a new request which means that the Chamber's ruling has to be handed down from case to case, from document to document, and this is also contained in the same decision in the Prlic case. Likewise, the decision of our Trial Chamber on page 10213, dated 26 February 2010, you, Your Honours, were of a position that such Prosecution requests have to be dealt with on a case-by-case basis. Page 10213, lines 6 through 8, which is where you rendered your decision on one such Prosecution's request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree that the Prlic decision is the guiding decision in this case. I agree with Mr. Lukic that the decisions in respect of each document have to be done on a case-by-case basis and on a document-by-document basis, so we have no disagreement. And I made submissions yesterday in respect of -- factual submissions in respect of this particular document. I would just like to make some additional factual submissions, if the Court deems it necessary. Let me just say in respect of this document: We received this document on the 29th of March, 2010. We disclosed it to the Defence by CD on the 9th of April, 2010, in other words, ten days after we received it. The diary is obviously in a language the accused understood and in a language that many members of his team understood. So there's no disadvantage to the Defence in respect of the language of the document itself. Indeed, we took a lengthy recess for the Defence and for the Prosecution to analyse these documents. We're offering this document now because it directly contradicts the evidence that has been presented by the witness. It's our submission there's no prejudice to the Defence whatsoever in the use of this document. We disclosed it, as I say, to the Defence on the 9th of April, 2010. We are seeking its admission in excess of three months after we disclosed it to the Defence. The content of the diary in substance -- the diary entry in substance is similar to three documents that we discussed yesterday, and that were 65 ter 6399, 65 ter 7346, and 65 ter 8948, so the substance is essentially the same. And it's our submission that there would be no prejudice to the Defence whatsoever from the admission of this document. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that Mr. Harmon has just explained that he wishes to use these documents in order to refute the testimony of witness Kovacevic, we agree that the documents should indeed be used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I don't mean to interrupt Your Honours, but I'm seeking the admission of this document - and if I spoke and mislead counsel, I apologise - but I'm seeking this document not only to impeach the witness but for the substance of the contents of the document. So I'm seeking it for both purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... if there is agreement of the parties [Microphone not activated] the Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the presiding, judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: If there is agreement for the parties, let me say that the Chamber has studied the case yesterday and conciles very much with both positions, both of the Defence and the Prosecution, so it is very important that, in introducing new evidence, fresh evidence, the justification should be made as a resolution cited by this Chamber by Mr. Lukic on a case-to-case basis; and also, let me remind all of you of the requirements of paragraph 24 and 25 of the Prlic decision. If that is the case, then we will call on the witness, and so we will proceed as you both have agree, and the ruling of the Chamber have approved. So, Mr. Registrar, let's bring the witness into the court. Let's go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness, I would like to regulate the status of the last exhibit that we were discussing. It was 65 ter 6399. I had concluded with that exhibit yesterday, and then we adjourned. I would like to move for its admission and ask that it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, let's admit the document into evidence and give an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P2916. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regards to the position -- I hope we remain in private session. With regards -- it's okay, I can do it generically enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the position that Mr. Harmon has taken concerning the admission of these documents, to the extent that Mr. Harmon seeks to introduce these documents for purposes of impeachment, we have no disagreement. With regard to them being introduced for other purposes, which Mr. Harmon has indicated that he does intend to do, we do have disagreement with regard to that. We do not believe that the threshold requirements have been made, and so the Chamber is very clear about this because it will most probably be the subject matter of some further litigation. We wish to lodge our objection with regard to that particular part of Mr. Harmon's presentation. For purposes of impeachment, we have no disagreement. For purposes of other purposes, we do have disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no comments, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: We take note of the objection, and if there is further discrepancies, the Chamber will rule on it. Thank you very much. MR. GUY SMITH: I appreciate the Chamber's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Let me remind you that you are still bound by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: -- your declaration in relation to the customary nature, and that we hope you had rested enough so to be also today very precise, concise, and just answering the precise points posed by both Prosecution and Defence when the re-examination comes. Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We were examining yesterday and I want to continue to examine your assertion that by the end of 1993 the VRS had sufficient quantities of ammunition and fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have XN 358 on the monitor, please. Well, I need the English version on the monitor. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, we should be in private session. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Let's be in private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Sir, what you have in front of you is an entry in General Mladic's diary, an entry of Tuesday the 17th of August, 1993, and it's a meeting, as you can see, of the inner circle of the VRS Main Staff. Sir, did you attend any Main Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally they did invite me from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you considered part of the inner circle of the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is a meeting, an internal meeting where these -- the people who were participating in this meeting are discussing topics that are listed on the agenda in front of you, item number 1 of which includes the situation in the Army of the RS, problems and how to solve them. And we can see on page 1 one of the participants was Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will see that General Gvero was a participant in these meetings. And -- I just want to quickly go through these pages so we can see who the participants were. If we go to the next page we see two persons named, one of whom is Colonel Sreto Kovacevic, and another is a Lieutenant-Colonel Dubovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, finally, if we can go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can see that a Colonel Miljanovic and General Milovanovic were noted, at least their comments were noted, during this meeting. Sir, I want to focus on the comments of Colonel Miljanovic on the 17th of August, 1993. Do you see -- and read that portion. Do you see where he states that the VRS logistics support is a problem as a whole, and he goes on to say that: "Materiel reserves have been exhausted, feeding the army is a problem, as are fuel and ammunition." You see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: From this document we can see that internally amongst the VRS Main Staff there were concerns and acknowledgments that the materiel reserves of the VRS as of August 17th had been exhausted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that what is written in here is correct. However, I can explain, if you give me a couple of minutes, and I can corroborate my statement that there was enough ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you just -- let me just go through some more documents. You can make an explanation at the conclusion of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to 65 ter -- no, I'm sorry, could I have an exhibit number for that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would suggest that the witness be allowed to answer the question so that there's sufficient -- there's a sufficient correlation to the information that's being discussed and this particular exhibit that it attends to. If Mr. Harmon is planning on showing the witness a number of documents thereafter, and we get a lengthy answer, I don't think that's necessarily an appropriate fashion to give clarity to the Chamber as to what is being discussed. There's also another problem with what has been done here which is that Mr. Harmon is asking for the witness to speculate with regard to what is involved in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to ask the witness, after I show him a series of documents, if he -- and I will give him an opportunity to comment on the documents I show him. I intend to show him about two or three more documents and then I'll give him an opportunity to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: At page 9, line 14, the witness said: "I believe that what is written here is correct, however, I can explain, if you give me a couple of minutes, and I can corroborate my statement that there was enough ammunition." Here we have, I believe, an option: Either to let the witness clarify a given issue posed by you, Mr. Harmon, which will add clarity to the situation, I imagine, or to later on give an overall explanation which may indeed lack clarity and precision. So my suggestion to you, Mr. Harmon, is to let the witness -- if there are pertinent comments, to do it on the occasion of the specific questions. And I would like to make a general comment that is not giving any one of the parties any direction, but I our transcripts, I was going through the transcript yesterday and days before, and it's becoming like a novel, you know, instead of very precise questions and very precise answers, it's going into a narrative of a narrative. And I think that for all the literary merits that it may have, we have a mandate here to be precise and to be concise and to be brief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, if you'd like to give your explanation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much for having given me the opportunity to provide an explanation to this central issue of my whole testimony. And allow me to remind this Honourable Trial Chamber that from 1972 up to 1992, for the whole 20 years, I was in charge of the ammunition depot in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in addition to all of the other parts of the infrastructure. I would also like to remind you that I participated and managed, towards the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, the mobilisation of depots --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object, the witness was going to give an explanation why he thought there was sufficient ammunition. I didn't ask him to give a description of his background. That's not responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please be concise and try to respond directly to the questions asked, because then if the parties are asking you questions, please do respond to the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. To be very specific: In the Rudo ammunition depot, in the Visegrad ammunition depot, in the Ustikolina ammunition depot, and in the Renovica ammunition depot, towards the end of 1991, there was anything between 16.000 and 19.000 tonnes of ammunition which belonged to the reserves of the Supreme Command of the JNA. About 50 per cent of that quantity -- or rather, between 8-, and 9.000 tonnes of ammunition from those depots were transported to the territory of Yugoslavia. About 8.000 tonnes remained either in the depots or most of it was distributed across the territory and stored in somewhat smaller depots. In Pecine, in caves, forests, and in some secret depots. In the month of November, I checked all those when I inspected the units deployed in the territory as a member of the commission that I've already spoken about earlier, and then we were able to confirm that in the general area of Podrinje there were about 8.000 tons of various kinds of ammunition. The second piece of information that I would like to share with you is the fact that in the Mrkonjic Grad depot, I personally saw that about 1.000 tonnes of different calibre of ammunition were stored there after having been transported from Slovenia and Croatia. About 1500 tonnes of ammunition had been brought over there from the Konjic and Gabela [phoen] depots. Also, about 1.000 tonnes of ammunition was transported there from the territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina which had previously been stored in the JNA depots, and, subsequently, all of that was taken over by the VRS. In the course of the war, nobody ever responded to my request and explain what had happened to that ammunition. Everybody knew that that ammunition had been distributed across the territory and that that ammunition was under the control of the local brigades and the local authorities. The prime minister himself, Mr. Lukic, he knew that very well. After the signing of the Dayton Accord, the peace forces located in the territory of Sokolac municipality in a village between Sokolac and Olovo, several dozens of hundreds of tonnes, and if I can remember properly, over 300 tonnes of ammunition and explosive, which proves that I am right. And this information was publicised by SFOR members. They destroyed all that in a cave in the area. When such a huge quantity exploded, it caused a small-scale earthquake, and the president of Sokolac municipality protested publicly on TV. He lodged a protest to the SFOR command, stating that the detonation had an impact on the source of the Bistrica River which was suppling Sokolac with water at the time. In the course of 1996 and 1997, SFOR units found huge quantities of ammunition hidden in the territory of Republika Srpska and confiscated all those. This is all a fact which can easily be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you count the facilities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, let me just ask you some questions about what you just said. Okay. You said there were secret depots and you checked those as a member of the commission that I had spoken about earlier. Which commission are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I explained yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just give me the name of the commission, if you would, sir. What was the name of the commission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission was established by the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Ratko Mladic. It was headed by Colonel Ilic, an operative officer within the staff, and I was a member of that commission. The task of that commission was to tour all the VRS units that were being set up or had already been set up by this time. My task was to determine the situation regarding the materiel reserves under all of the logistical aspects. I can also explain about the secret depots if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness addressed this on day two of his testimony, but just to be precise for the sake of the transcript, maybe we should specify the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, specify the year, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in September 1992. That's when the commission began its work. We concluded our work sometime in late November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And was that the last time that you personally inspected those secret depots and locations that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that level of complexity, yes, only then. I did, later, tour individual locations though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we're talking about the sufficiency of ammunition, sir, at the end of 1993. And I would like now to take you to another document, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 7346 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: There is no interpretation to what Mr. Lukic has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't hear either. I did not get an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this one of the three documents that Mr. Harmon mentioned yesterday; and, if so, may we know the reason for its use?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The reason -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Before Mr. Harmon speaks, let me remind you that judge -- my colleague and myself recalled that we have accepted by majority yesterday these documents with the dissent of Judge Moloto. I just want to remind the parties of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me proceed with this document. General, this is a document -- we'll identify the document first. This is a document that is dated the 1st of November, 1993. It's from the VRS Main Staff. It is a top secret, and it is addressed to the government of the Republika Srpska. And the topic is, "Problems of Logistic Support for the Army."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to the end of the document, we'll see who the author of this document was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You see a name and a signature. Can you tell us whose name it is and whose signature it is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go back to the -- could we go to the second page of the English, please. And the second page of the -- I'm sorry, the first page of the B/C/S. Okay, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We should be in public session on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, I hope that I am correct, but at the bottom of the Serbian language version of this document it should read -- it starts, a paragraph: "The materiel reserves of the army..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm directing Your Honours' attention to the second paragraph in the English language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This says that the materiel -- General Mladic tells the government that: "The materiel reserves of the army, as the main source of supply from the beginning of the war until the present, have been exhausted ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page of the Serbian language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you'll see, General, that the first bullet point item down below that paragraph following the words, The current problems of logistics support, besides the ones listed, are as follows: "Out of a total of 23 items, the army has no reserves for 15 of them." And it lists various perishable products. Then if we go two paragraphs down, he says to the government: "Of 148 types of ammunition, 35 per cent of these, the reserves of artillery and PA ammunition, is zero." Can you tell us what "PA" stands for?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stands for anti-aircraft ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And on your document this should be visible to you, sir. The penultimate bullet point says: "The reserves of tires, batteries, covers for vehicle, spare parts for combat," and it goes on to list a series of items, "are on a zero level or on minimum." And finally he says: "The level of supplies of medicines, sanitary materials, and other items are below the necessary minimum." So in this document we can see that General Mladic is addressing the government, expressing that there are in fact serious deficiencies in the reserves that are available to him; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic that vouches for this information. Nevertheless, when this data was entered into his report, the commodity reserves were not taken into account, and that was where the army's reserves of foodstuffs, medicine, and fuel were kept, and everything else, all of their basic necessities with the exception of ammunition. Furthermore, the ministries of finance or Defence were not consulted either, and obviously their information might have affected the totals as given here. They could have told him, General, sir, your information is not correct. So what this reflects is information as known by the Main Staff but not as known by other participants who may have had helpful information to contribute to this review.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have two exhibit numbers. I failed to ask for an exhibit number for XN 358, and could I also have an exhibit number for this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall -- the 65 ter XN 358 shall be assigned Exhibit P2917. 65 ter document 7346 shall be assigned Exhibit P2918. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Kovacevic, at the end of 1993, the future supply of ammunition was a matter of critical importance for the VRS and for your government; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that only applied to certain types of ammunition. To be used for replenishing the reserves of the Main Staff. It was units up to brigade or corps level that used that type of the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what types of ammunition? When you say, I think that only applied to certain types of ammunition that were of critical importance to the VRS and to your government, what types of ammunition then were of critical importance?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7.62 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Any other types?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12.7 millimetre for anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So those were only two types of critical ammunition that were of concern to your government and to the VRS? Is that what I understand your testimony to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just wait a minute, Witness, just -- I'm sorry. There's a conversation up here. If you just wait a minute. Please give your answer. Oh, I see Mr. Lukic is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am standing because I think there is a discrepancy between the questions and answers. I think it's something to do with the interpretation and could Mr. Harmon please re-ask his question just to make sure there's no confusion. What exactly does he mean by critical ammunition and what exactly does the witness mean? I suppose the purpose is to find out what ammunition, what type of ammunition was in short supply. There seems to be a bit of confusion that has arisen from the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before you answer the question, these two documents, P2917, should it go under seal?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Harmon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 2917 should be under seal, Your Honour; and 2918, there's no reason that it be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, General, let me just start again. I want to be perfectly clear. I asked you a question at page 18, line 14: "At the end of 1993, the future supply of ammunition was a matter of critical importance for the VRS and your government." Your answer was: "I think that only applied to certain types of ammunition." Then I asked you what types of ammunition that applied to. And you've given us 7.62 and 12.7 millimetres. And my question to you is: Are those the only two types of ammunition that that were of critical importance to the the VRS and to your government from -- for the period of 1993 on to 1995? Or, sir, was it the case that all types of ammunition were of critical importance if the VRS was to prosecute the war to its conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The type of ammunition most badly needed by the army was the 7.62 millimetre for the automatic rifle, the Kalashnikov; for the semi-automatic, 7.62. For the M-84 machine-gun, again 7.62. These are weapons that were part of the armoury of the soldiers along the front line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the last sentence. The interpreter did not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was some types of artillery ammunition too, such as the 130 and 122 millimetres. Nevertheless, one believed that the army was supposed to stop any attacks, organise the defence, and resume the peace talks --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me, I'm going to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the production at Vogosca --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Harmon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you about the types of ammunition that were critical. I merely asked to you identify those. I want to carry on, and I would like to conclude today. Sir, I would like to show you another document then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could P2766 on the monitor. P2766.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you go into -- I was advised that this document is confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was just checking on that, Your Honour. I had not been advised that's the case. Yes, then, Your Honour, we should. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: We shall go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, let's start by identifying this document. This is a document that's dated the 15th of May, 1994, from President Karadzic to General Perisic, personally. It's directed to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. And you can see that in the top portion of the document. I would like to direct your attention, sir, to a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The Court's attention, first of all, Your Honour. If we could go to the bottom of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in your version, do you see a portion that starts: "Our army is exhausted and stretched"? It should be toward the bottom of your -- do you see that portion of the document, General Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: President Karadzic informs General Perisic five months into 1994: "Our army is exhausted and stretched out over a long front line. This too could be overcome, however, but the shortage of every" - and I emphasise the word "every" here, sir - "type of ammunition cannot be overcome but through the provision of ammunition. At some military lines, our soldiers are awaiting enemy infantry attacks with just one or two ammunition clips in their automatic rifles respectively." So this document, General Kovacevic, from the president of the Republika Srpska to the chief of the VJ General Staff General Perisic says that there's a shortage of every type of ammunition. And every type of ammunition -- strike that. Can you comment on that, sir? Is General -- is President Karadzic mistaken as well as General Mladic was previously and General Milovanovic was previously?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept the wording here that all types of ammunition were exhausted. Karadzic himself claims that there is ammunition but no more than two rounds per soldier. It is entirely impossible to assume that all - and when I say "all," I mean really all - reserves of ammunition had been exhausted by this time. That is simply not true. There were some types of ammunition that posted a problem. That much is true. The extra supplies that we got were a bare minimum, nevertheless one cannot use a blanket statement like this and apply it to all different types of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm finished with this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, General Kovacevic, from August of 1994 until the end of the war, that was a period when there was the largest consumption of combat materiel, ammunition and the like; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The consumption was greater than in the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you spoke to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Actually, I think we can go back now into public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Public session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, when you spoke with Office of the Prosecutor representatives in 2007, you made the following statement, and I want to see if you stand by this. You said: "Especially" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just -- the page reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. It's in page 61 of 2007, the second interview. I'm referring to page 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, you said: "Especially in 1995, more combat materiel was spent than in 1994, especially compared to 1993 because during this period, from August 1994 until the end of the war, the biggest combat operations took place. There was Podrinje, Srebrenica, there was the defence of the western municipalities." And you described, then, some additional areas of combat operations. Do you still stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At page 62, you also -- of that interview - for counsel's benefit, 62 of the English of the same interview. You said: "I'm going back to what I said, August 1994 til the end of the war in 1995, that was the period when the greatest combat operations were carried out with the most resources spent, fuel, victims, and everything else in that period." Sir, do you still stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we talked yesterday about the embargo, the economic embargo that was commenced on the 4th of August, 1994, as a result of the Vance Owen -- the Contact Group plan not being accepted. In fact, despite that embargo, General Kovacevic, goods flowed across the Drina River from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia into Republika Srpska every day, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some goods did flow. For example, oil, cigarettes, some types of foods and other goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, in addition to those types of goods, military goods flowed across the border. And, in fact, the embargo in respect of the transportation of military goods from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia into the Republika Srpska was an illusion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain by way of saying that that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am commenting on the president's document with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Are you saying that -- let me see if I can understand your answer. Did military goods, during the time of the embargo - I'm talking about military goods including ammunition, artillery shells, mines, and the like - did they -- were they transported across the Drina River from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia into the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that those types of goods could not flow freely across the border, because at every border crossing there were international monitors deployed. It would have been absolutely impossible, and it is a full statement on anybody's part if they say that such goods could flow freely. There were attempts to transport ammunition from Serbia to Republika Srpska; however, I don't know whether that was indeed done or, if it was, who did it. My participation in the whole matter was defined pursuant to an order by Radovan Karadzic, the then-president of the republic. And together with some other people, we were supposed to establish whether it was possible to transport ammunition from Serbia to Republika Srpska across the existing border crossings. And the dead-line we were given was seven days. I personally drafted a report for President Karadzic in which I informed him that it was impossible to transport any convoys across the border, and I also stated what control bodies operated on those border crossings, but I also said that there might be somebody who could transport one, two, three, our four trucks at the most. I told him that I didn't want to continue being involved in that job because I did not have any authority either over the police or the military. And then he said, Okay, the military will do that. And that's where my knowledge about the whole matter stops.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony that from the time of the embargo, August the 4th, 1994, you are not aware of any ammunition, artillery shells, mines being transported from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia into the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did learn at the session of the commission that we discussed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mean, you learned that at the session of the commission you've just described, that some ammunition had come across the Drina River from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia into the RS? Is that when you first learned of this development?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received such information, and we entered the information into our own reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the commission that you talked about was a commission that was formed on the 20th of June, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's take a look at, then -- if I could have P -- I'm sorry, P2726, please. Actually, let me start with P2851. I need to go into private session. Apparently this is confidential. This is under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Take a look at that document, if you will, General Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- the document is self-explanatory, and no further comment is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. The embargo restricted economic transactions, did it not yes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Could we go to Prosecution Exhibit 1257, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that is dated the 27th of February, and if you read the first paragraph, it says: "On the basis of ruling conf. number 85-7 of 24/02.1995, the chief of the VJ General Staff, please issue to the 30th Personnel Centre from VP 5292 Mrsac the following:" And it describes 100 rounds of howitzer cannon ammunition, and -- do you see that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it says that -- below that, it says, the description of the ordnance, it says that the transport of the ammunition from Kragujevac will be taken over by the owned vehicle. So the owned vehicle that we are talking about is -- I mean -- strike that. This particular ammunition was sent to the VRS in the Republika Srpska, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is actually an order for the ammunition to be handed over to the VRS. However, it doesn't transpire from the document that the order ever materialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: It's time to adjourn. If we are in open session, let's do so. Court adjourns until quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Kovacevic, what I'd like to do is just show you a series of documents, and I'm going to invite you to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecution Exhibit 2726 on the monitor. This is under seal, I'm told. No, I'm sorry, public. So could this be on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, this is a document that's dated the 19th of June, 1995, and it is addressed to the General Staff of the VJ to the attention of the chief of the General Staff of the VJ. And it is from the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska. Now, this is a document that, as you can see below, it's a support in ammunition, it's a request. And you'll see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a request for various types of ammunition, including a million and a half pieces of 7.62 automatic rifle -- semi-automatic rifle ammunition; and 7.62 machine-gun rifle, 200.000 rounds; and other types of ordnance. And it is a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us from -- who is -- who signed this document or who's type-signed as the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The author of the document is Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page of the English, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you'll see that -- actually let me do something else. Can you read --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the wrong page in the English, I apologise. If we could go to the previous page in the English, we'll come back to this page in a moment. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a request, and you'll see at the bottom of the document it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We need to go to the last page in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You'll see in this document that the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia cabinet of the chief of the General Staff has agreed to the request. And I want to correct the translation that appears in this document because the English translation says in the second line of the text, it says: "... inform you that the Chief of the VRS Main Staff ordered," and that should be VJ instead of VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Lukic can assist me in that, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to what Mr. Harmon has just said, and that can be found in paragraph 30, line 8. I'm not going to suggest a question to the witness, however, if Mr. Harmon says that it has been approved, could he please be more specific and tell us based on what.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, let's deal with the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Harmon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me deal with one item at a time. I've pointed out an error in the translation, and I have said that this is improperly translated in English to read that "the chief of the VRS Main Staff ordered, Give it to Ratko and have this solved." "VRS" should be "VJ."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic asked me on what this is based.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, when the chief of -- from this document, General Kovacevic, the chief of -- General Perisic approved this request, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from the document that General Perisic ordered that that should be handed over to Ratko to deal with it. A Ratko who was in charge of dealing with this, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then we'll move on to the next exhibit. If I could have P --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There are two exhibits I'm going to ask you to comment on. I'm going to show them both to you, and then I'm going to invite your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have, first of all, P2746 on the monitor. And that will be followed by P951. So if we could start with 2746.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document as you can see is dated the 7th of October, 1995, and it is a document from the VRS Main Staff. And you can see on the -- the person who sent it is Ratko Mladic. It's a request for ten FAB-275/4. Those are aerial bombs, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of equipment that is. Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So as the minister of defence you're unfamiliar with what an FAB-275/4 is? You are not familiar with that description?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that that was not part of the armament of the land forces of Republika Srpska, and I don't know that even during the JNA era that was part of the land forces. That must be some sort of lethal weaponry pertaining to the area of anti-aircraft defence, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. If we take a look at the reference number in the upper left-hand corner, you'll see 03/4-2618, which is the reference number for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next page, please, in the English. And I think we're fine on the Serbian language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You see that there is an entry dated the 7th of October, 1995, that reads: "The Chief of the General Staff VJ has approved for the General Staff of the VRS to be resolved as soon as possible. Please send your reply." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It says to the air force and entire aircraft defence sector, the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia approved for the Army Republika Srpska General Staff to be resolved as soon as possible. Feedback is requested. Whether the matter had been dealt with in the air force and anti-aircraft defence command of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have P951 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that relates to the previous document I showed you. We can see that by the reference number referring to the telegram number 03/4-2618 of 7 October 1995. And in this document, this says that the collection of these FAB-275/4 has been approved and that they can be collected from the 608th Logistics Base. And this is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia General Staff informing the republic -- the VRS Main Staff of that fact. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we turn to the next document, please. This is P2781, dated the 12th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection. If you could bear with me just for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document shown by Mr. Harmon is one of those that we didn't know anything about. We didn't know that it would be discussed with this witness; therefore, I would kindly request for the question and the answer not to be taken into account in respect of the document in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have to check to see if that is, in fact, the case with my records. Nevertheless, this document that -- I take it that Mr. Lukic is objecting to 951. This document is one that is referenced in a document he was notified of, P2746. So he is on notice or he did get the document 2746, so I make that observation. I also make the observation, Your Honour: Mr. Lukic also had documents that he did not have on his list, and I had an opportunity to review that technical violation of the Rules, and after reviewing those documents I was perfectly satisfied to have Mr. Lukic to proceed with the documents. I'm -- frankly, surprised at this objection, but Mr. Lukic has the right to make the objection, but I'm surprised given that he has already received 2746 that he objects to the related document of P951. I think, Your Honour, it is in the interest of justice to have this document heard. It's been presented to the witness. I think there's sufficient notice, although a technical violation, I concede, but there's been sufficient notice as to the substance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to take this opportunity to respond to Mr. Harmon. Under the Rules and your instructions, we have to give notice at least two days before a witness appears in the courtroom to the OTP about any documents that we may be using, which I duly complied. The first list that I worked with contained between 30 and 40 documents, and I served the list on the OTP three days before the witness appeared. And then there were several additional documents that I informed them of, at least the day before the witness appeared in this courtroom. We are talking about these documents, but there is another thing that the Trial Chamber doesn't know about because we have not so far drawn anyone's attention to this ever since the start of the Defence case when the OTP serves on us a list of documents that they intend to use during their cross. They tend to provide very extensive lists, specifically in relation to Mr. Kovacevic. Yesterday, when the cross-examination began, I received a list containing 157 documents that the OTP apparently intended to use with this witness. We cannot accept the fact that if this document was introduced along with another document and was not on the list, it should now be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm in your hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: The Chamber has been alerted by both parties that somewhat this situation has not been presented before due to the fact that both parties have some kind of agreement on how to proceed in relation to certain documents as I understood by Mr. Harmon. Could you, Mr. Harmon, give the Chamber additional explanations on how the situation is just, in many respects, a novel situation because before you had an agreement with the Defence on the presentation of documents which has not been referenced directly but through another one, you think this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we obviously give the Defence lists of documents when we start our cross-examination. What the objection is -- and I don't want to spend a lot of time on this, Your Honour, from an evidentiary points of view, because I want to try to get through this witness today and give Mr. Lukic plenty of time to examine the witness if he feels necessary. We give lists. Mr. Lukic has said we give large lists. We give large lists precisely for the reason that we don't want to confront an objection like this should we find the need arise to a use of a document. This document was not given to Mr. Lukic, apparently, by omission. The companion document was. We have an agreement, and there's a technical violation, if you will, of the agreement. Mr. Lukic, we also have guide-lines. The guide-lines that apply to the Defence giving us documents were breached in the course of this examination of this witness. As I say, that was, I think, two days ago. The fact of the matter is, some documents take the parties by surprise and warrant an objection. My submission is, this document, a technical violation of the agreement that we have with the Defence, is not a document that could have taken him by surprise because it is referenced in the companion document. So that's why I am surprised by this objection. I think I -- have I responded to Your Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Harmon claims that this is an error, and since the document has been shown and the witness responded, my reaction was late and I will therefore have to withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Could we have Prosecution Exhibit 623, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document, sir, that is dated the 15th of May, it is from Military Post 4919 in Belgrade, and it is a consent on engineers, weapons, and military equipment to be handed over to the VRS based on the approval of the chief of the VJ General Staff. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the information in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any comment on it, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment is, I wonder why the VJ was asked to provide these mines, knowing that there were over 10.000 mines like this throughout the war in the Koran depot at Pale. The same situation applied after the war. A portion was destroyed when the depot was targeted by NATO. It simply can't be true that these weapons were in short supply. That is why I say the request surprises me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to Prosecution Exhibit 2731, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document from the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army Office of the Chief of the General Staff, and it's dated the 28th of June, 1995, and it is addressed to the command of the 2nd Army, assistant commander for logistics. Now, the 2nd Army is a VJ unit, and we've heard evidence about that. But you can see from this document, sir, that the chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, is ordered that the requested assets, which are 200 grad motors, be given to the VRS. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what a grad motor is? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, and I'm not quite sure, these are motors for launching anti-hail rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, were you aware that the VRS was using aerial bombs in its bombardment of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that, aside from what I read in the media about the shelling itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Right. Sir, let me take you to Prosecution Exhibit 1205, please. Okay, sir, this is a document -- the date is not evident on the first page, it's evident on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page just to see the date. It's 30th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. You see that at the bottom? You confirm that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads: "At the command of the Majevica Tactical Group, the 30th of June, 1995, at 10 .00 a.m. Lieutenant-Colonel Milenko Kovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this document is in relation to the take-over of Yugoslav Army vehicles, and there's -- it refers to a decision on the schedule of the take-over, which is the 5th of July, 1995. What I'm particularly interested in this document to discuss with you and is something that you touched upon was -- is in subpart 4 of this document, because this is a document that's talking about transporting 22 motor vehicles and 5 trailers, so it's a significant number of assets. But read paragraph 4, if you will. This says that: "Prepare the IBK ..." What does "IBK" stand for?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an engineering unit. I think they are specifically building a pontoon bridge here, the kind used to get across rivers. So there's a pontoon bridge being set up by engineering units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a pontoon bridge being set up by a VJ engineering unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Mr. Lukic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not sure how happy he can possibly be with this, it reads "IBK." I thought you wanted to know what that means, IBK, the abbreviation, what it stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the interpretation perhaps made it a little more confusing. Perhaps the witness should explain the acronym.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Very briefly General, what does "IBK" stand for?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't come across the acronym, so I didn't even comment on it. It's not that it was confusing. But it stands for East Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So the East Bosnia Corps is part of the VRS, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It's a corps of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it says then: "Prepare the East Bosnia Corps engineer battalion pontoon unit for carrying out the task (selecting men, setting aside MS" - which stands for materiel supplies - "reconnoitering the crossing point, make arrangements for a check-point and access road, prepare an area for camouflaging amphibian) the commander of the DD Border Detachment ..." Let me stop there. The Drina Division Border Detachment, sir, which army is that associated with?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Border detachment, DD, I really can't be specific about what it means. If this was the VJ, it would probably be VJ, V=D, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me read on. "The commander of the DD Border Detachment proposes that the takeover be carried out in the sector of the village of Balatu-Crna Barai. Illegal crossings are the least frequent there. Access roads are good. The Drina River bed has no dunes, and the crossing point is easy to close off to prevent the UNPROFOR from coming ..." Sir, military goods from the VJ and from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did travel through to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a result of covert -- of efforts to conceal the delivery of necessary munitions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This reads, specifically, that the bridge should be set up for crossings. It's easy to close off and it's easy to make the crossing, but it doesn't specifically state that the crossing would be used to transport munition. There were quite many illegal crossings, especially for fuel, livestock, cigarettes. This may have been used for such a purpose as well. Nevertheless, I can't say I've ever read about ammunition or any other type of ordnance being transported here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. Okay. I won't go further on this document. Let me change the topic slightly, sir. In your earlier testimony, you testified that you had been appointed to a state committee for the procurement of arms for the Republika Srpska, and that was in 1995; is that correct? That calls for a yes or no answer, sir. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, but the name of the document as stated by you is inaccurate. And if you want me to, I can set the record straight on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please do that, General.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a state committee for centralised procurement to the armed forces of Republika Srpska. I believe you have that document in your possession, and I'm sure that's how the header reads. Nevertheless, it certainly doesn't say anywhere that the procurement committee was set up from Yugoslavia, only from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't say that, but lets me proceed with this document. You are correct; I do have it. I'm holding it in my hand, General, and I want to confirm that the members of that committee were Radovan Karadzic; Ratko Mladic; Momcilo Krajisnik; Dusan Cosic, who was the prime minister; Milan Ninkovic, who you mentioned was the SDS successor, minister of defence; Ranko Pajic, the minister of finance; and Tomo Kovac, who was the deputy minister of Internal Affairs. They were the members appointed to the committee, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the task of the committee was to provide centralised procurement for the armed forces of the Republika Srpska in weapons and ammunition, power forces, food supplies, quartermaster and medical equipment and instruments, materiel equipment, spare parts, and expendable materiel. That was one of the tasks of the committee; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Interested -- if I could have -- let me ask you this question, sir: You mentioned yesterday that you were on a part of a committee, and in fact you mentioned this this morning in your evidence, that you were part of a committee, an executive team, to examine transport means of getting materiel from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Do you remember your earlier testimony this morning?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the secretary of that committee. I had no powers except to gather reports and records such as received by the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring to your evidence, sir. It is found on page 25, starting at line 6. You said, in respect of transportation of ammunition from Serbia to the republic, you said: There were attempts to transport ammunition from Serbia to the Republika Srpska, however, I didn't know -- I'm sorry, let me start at line 8: "My participation in the whole matter was defined pursuant to an order by Radovan Karadzic, the then-president of the republic. And together with some other people, we were supposed to establish whether it was possible to transport ammunition from Serbia to Republika Srpska across the existing border crossings. And the dead-line ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Harmon slow down, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "And the dead-line we were given was seven days. "I personally drafted a report for President Karadzic in which I informed him that it was impossible to transport any convoys across the border, and I also stated that controlled bodies operated on those border crossings, but I said that there might be somebody who could transport one, two, three, or four trucks at most. I told him that I didn't want to continue being involved in that job because I did not have any authority either over the police or the military. And then he said, Okay, the military will do that. And that's where my knowledge about the whole thing stops." Now, that's what you testified this morning, and I want to ask you questions about that committee that you were the team leader of, General. That was -- there was an executive team that was established to look at ways in which materiel could be transported; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the other members of that team were General -- Lieutenant-Colonel Miroslav Cvijetic, Milenko Serenic [phoen], Branko Prodanovic [phoen], Momcilo Mandic, and Veselinka Toruntas [phoen], as well as Mirko Krajisnik. Now, Mirko Krajisnik was the brother of Momcilo Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the task of the team was to organise and transport relevant means from the FRY within the next seven days and place them in the locations which were agreed on. Now, my question to you, sir, is: The transport of what? What was your executive team looking at to transport from the FRY into the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was ammunition to be used by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And where were the locations that were agreed upon where this ammunition would be deposited or brought to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ammunition should have been delivered to the logistics base in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was this the formation of this committee in -- as a result of contemplated continued military activities that would require ammunition and logistical support?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object. I believe that the question is compound, complex. Could it please be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the team that you were the team leader of, was that created because the VRS needed additional logistical support transported from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received an order to try and see or investigate whether the ammunition could be transported across the border or not. That's the only thing I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the ammunition was going to be used by the VRS in future military operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wasn't aware of any operations. It was simply to be used to replenish the VRS equipment and means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And you were made the executive team leader pursuant to a decision that was issued on the 20th of June, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is correct, and the document was in effect for no more than seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And on the 20th of June, 1995, that was approximately three weeks before the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, which you know about, isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible, but I was unaware of any operation in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you learn about the -- as minister of defence, when was it that you learned about the operation against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was removed from the position as defence minister in August 1994, or, rather, the end of July 1994. Before then and up to then, I'm sure I did not become aware of anything going on in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were the deputy minister of defence because you told us that, so when did -- my question to you, sir, is: When did you learn about the operation that was conducted by the VRS against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a secret operation. Only a small number of people were privy to the information about that operation. I'm sure that I didn't know anything prior to the operation starting. I learned about it only in August 1995, not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When, in August of 1995, did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that when Operation Storm was either already completed or still underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you give us a date or approximate date? Was it in the beginning of August, the end of August, the middle of August?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the president of the republic issued an order to assign me to the group which was charged with billeting the Main Staff of the VRS on Mount Kozara in hotel Kozara near Prijedor. That was sometime in mid-August or in the first half of the month of August, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Sir, let me ask you, I told you yesterday that I would come back to the question of Mr. Ecimovic who was the technical director at Pretis factory. After the war, sir, did he return to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know Aleksa Krsmanovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Colonel Aleksa Krsmanovic rather well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps assistant commander for organisation and mobilisation during the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his position during the war in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was assistant commander for logistics in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So he was in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command then but for logistics issues?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. He was in the command and he was dealing with the logistics issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to change the topic. I want to ask you about something that you said in your testimony earlier. You said in the transcript at 12729, lines 11 through 14, you said: "I have never heard of a procedure where the Army of Yugoslavia would have jurisdiction or the VJ courts would have jurisdiction in relation to any breaches of discipline committed in the VRS." That was your testimony. Let me ask you, first of all: Was a -- was going AWOL, abandoning your unit, in the VRS considered a breach of discipline under the VJ RS Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have P2423 on the monitor. Let me just check to see if that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we have an error in the transcript. "VJ RS Law on the Army"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. That is wrong. Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was going AWOL or abandoning your unit considered a disciplinary offence under the army law of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every disciplinary offence committed by a VRS member fell under the regulations governing the work of disciplinary courts and subsequently the military courts of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question was: Was going AWOL or abandoning one's unit in the VRS a disciplinary offence? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Prosecution Exhibit 2423 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
